questions.x: Reflection fixed more answers without bringing confidence into line with accuracy. Getting more right and knowing how sure to be are separate outcomes, and the technique helped only the first.

questions.t: "A door badge opens the lab only if it has been activated. This badge hasn't been activated. So it won't open the lab." Restated as an if-then, this is modus tollens, so the form is valid.
questions.f: "A door badge opens the lab only if it has been activated. This badge hasn't been activated. So it won't open the lab." Restated as an if-then, this denies the antecedent, so the form is invalid.
questions.x: "P only if Q" means "if P then Q": if the badge opens the lab, it has been activated. The second premise denies that consequent, so concluding the antecedent is false is valid. Normalise "only if" before judging the form.

questions.t: Every modus tollens argument can be rewritten as a modus ponens on the contrapositive, "if not Q then not P", which is why both forms are valid.
questions.f: Every modus tollens argument can be rewritten as a modus ponens on the converse, "if Q then P", which is why both forms are valid.
questions.x: A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, so denying Q and applying "if not Q then not P" gives not-P by modus ponens. The converse is not equivalent, and reasoning from it is how affirming the consequent goes wrong.

questions.t: In a 2005 study of 120 students, 83% accepted the modus ponens conclusion as certain but only 50% accepted the modus tollens one.
questions.f: In a 2005 study of 120 students, 83% accepted the modus tollens conclusion as certain but only 50% accepted the modus ponens one.
questions.x: Markovits and Handley found modus tollens much harder, a gap that persisted when people rated probabilities instead. Handling the negated consequent is where people stumble, even though the form is just as valid.

questions.t: Sure her new pricing page lifted sales, a manager cites the weeks sales rose and three happy customer emails, but never checks sales in regions that kept the old page. That is confirmation bias.
questions.f: Sure her new pricing page lifted sales, a manager cites the weeks sales rose and three happy customer emails, but never checks sales in regions that kept the old page. That is belief perseverance.
questions.x: She only runs checks that could agree with her, so her confidence grows without the idea ever being at risk. Belief perseverance is holding on to a belief after its supporting evidence has been discredited, which hasn't happened here.

questions.t: To check a hunch about why a metric moved, write down at least one rival explanation and ask how likely each piece of evidence would be under each one.
questions.f: To check a hunch about why a metric moved, list every piece of evidence that fits the hunch and ask how strongly each one supports it.
questions.x: Evidence that would look the same whether you're right or wrong shouldn't raise your confidence. Comparing explanations side by side exposes that; collecting fits for one idea is the bias itself.

questions.t: Guess and Coppock's three large survey experiments found no evidence that counter-attitudinal information makes people dig in harder, even under conditions designed to favour backlash.
questions.f: Guess and Coppock's three large survey experiments found strong evidence that counter-attitudinal information makes people dig in harder, especially under conditions designed to favour backlash.
questions.x: The core tendency to favour congenial information is well supported, but the stronger "backfire" claim attached to it has not held up. Presenting contrary evidence is not usually counterproductive.

questions.t: Before a board meeting, the chief of staff quietly keeps a critical consultant's report off the agenda so the CEO's plan isn't "distracted." In Janis's groupthink model, she is acting as a mindguard.
questions.f: Before a board meeting, the chief of staff quietly keeps a critical consultant's report off the agenda so the CEO's plan isn't "distracted." In Janis's groupthink model, she is showing the illusion of invulnerability.
questions.x: A mindguard screens unwelcome information out of the group, one of Janis's pressure-toward-uniformity symptoms. The illusion of invulnerability is the group overrating itself, an excess optimism rather than an act of filtering.
